title: Gleevec and targeted cancer drugs

confidence.note: The approval date is on the FDA record, and the chain from the Philadelphia chromosome to the BCR-ABL gene to imatinib is well documented in the published literature.

people: Peter Nowell, University of Pennsylvania pathologist
David Hungerford, graduate student and his collaborator
Brian Druker, Oregon oncologist who led the first clinical trial
Nicholas Lydon, head of a pharmaceutical drug-discovery group
summary: A short chromosome spotted in 1960 led, four decades later, to a pill that turned a fatal leukemia into a manageable condition.
body: In 1960 Peter Nowell and David Hungerford, studying leukemia cells in Philadelphia, noticed that one chromosome was abnormally short. Later work showed that this "Philadelphia chromosome" fuses two genes, BCR and ABL, and that the hybrid drives chronic myeloid leukemia. In the 1990s the oncologist Brian Druker and Nicholas Lydon's drug-discovery team found a compound that blocks the rogue protein. The FDA approved it as imatinib (Gleevec) on 10 May 2001, after a review of only ten weeks. More than 70 similar kinase-blocking drugs have followed.

links.note: The older approach: poisons that kill dividing cells indiscriminately.
The other big shift in cancer drugs since 2000.

title: SARS

confidence.note: WHO's final tally covers probable cases with onset between 1 November 2002 and 31 July 2003. Counts are of probable cases, so they depend on case definitions that differed between countries.

place: China, Vietnam, Hong Kong, Canada and elsewhere
people: Carlo Urbani (1956–2003), WHO infectious-disease specialist in Hanoi
summary: A new coronavirus jumped continents by plane in 2003, killed the doctor who raised the alarm, and reshaped the global rules for reporting outbreaks.
body: The first known case of severe acute respiratory syndrome fell ill in China in November 2002. On 28 February 2003 Carlo Urbani, a WHO specialist in Hanoi, examined a businessman with a strange pneumonia, recognized the danger and alerted WHO. He caught the disease and died on 29 March. By July WHO had counted 8,096 probable cases and 774 deaths, 1,706 of the cases in health workers. SARS showed how governments could hide outbreaks, as China at first did; the revised International Health Regulations adopted in May 2005 let WHO use unofficial reports to counter that.

links.note: A rehearsal, imperfectly learned, for a far larger coronavirus pandemic.
WHO's role in coordinating the response.

title: The HPV vaccine

confidence.note: The 2006 US approval is well documented. The fall in cervical cancer comes from national registry data in vaccinated cohorts, which are still young, so the long-term size of the effect is still being measured.

people: Harald zur Hausen, German virologist, Nobel Prize 2008
Ian Frazer, immunologist at the University of Queensland
Jian Zhou (d. 1999), virologist who made the virus-like particles
summary: A virus was shown to cause cervical cancer, two scientists in Brisbane built empty virus shells, and a vaccine now prevents most cases.
body: Against the prevailing view, Harald zur Hausen argued that a papillomavirus caused cervical cancer, and in 1983 found a new type, HPV16, in tumor biopsies; types 16 and 18 turned up in about 70% of cervical cancers. In 1991 Ian Frazer and Jian Zhou in Brisbane reported that the virus's capsid proteins could self-assemble into harmless virus-like particles, the basis of the vaccines. Zhou died in 1999. The first vaccine, Gardasil, was approved in the United States in June 2006. In England, women offered vaccination at 12–13 now have around 80% less cervical cancer.

links.note: The earlier vaccine against a virus-caused cancer.
Screening, the other half of cervical-cancer prevention.

title: The microbiome

confidence.note: The project's dates and the C. difficile trial are well documented. Most claimed links between gut microbes and other diseases rest on associations whose causal role is unproven.

summary: Sequencing revealed the microbes living in and on us. The clearest cure so far came from an old idea: transplanting stool.
body: From 2007 to 2016 the NIH's Human Microbiome Project built DNA-sequence catalogs of the microbes living on and in healthy people, and NIH microbiome funding elsewhere grew more than forty-fold. The firmest clinical result came from an older, unglamorous idea. In a 2013 randomized trial, infusing donor stool cured recurrent *Clostridioides difficile* infection so much better than antibiotics that the trial was stopped early; the FDA approved the first stool-based products in 2022 and 2023. For irritable bowel syndrome and colitis, guidelines still recommend fecal transplants only within trials, and critics warn the field needs skepticism.

links.note: Cheap sequencing made the census of microbes possible.
C. difficile thrives after antibiotics wipe out normal gut bacteria.

title: Cancer immunotherapy

confidence.note: Regulatory approvals and the Nobel citation are documented. Coley's results were never confirmed by controlled trials, and modern drugs help some patients far more than others.

place: New York; Kyoto, Japan; and elsewhere
people: William B. Coley (1862–1936), New York bone-sarcoma surgeon
James P. Allison, immunologist, Nobel Prize 2018
Tasuku Honjo, immunologist, Nobel Prize 2018
summary: A century after a surgeon injected tumors with bacteria, drugs that release the immune system's brakes made the idea work.
body: In 1891 the New York surgeon William Coley, struck by tumors that shrank after a bacterial skin infection, began injecting cancer patients with bacteria, later a mixture of killed streptococci and the germ now called *Serratia marcescens*. Many physicians doubted his results, and the mechanism was a mystery.

The revival came from finding the immune system's brakes. In 1992 Tasuku Honjo discovered PD-1, a protein on T cells. James Allison showed at the end of 1994 that an antibody blocking another brake, CTLA-4, cured mice with cancer. The anti-CTLA-4 drug ipilimumab was approved in the United States and Europe in 2011 for advanced melanoma, and anti-PD-1 drugs followed in 2014, first in Japan. Allison and Honjo shared the 2018 Nobel Prize.

A second approach, CAR-T therapy, genetically re-engineers a patient's own T cells to attack cancer; the first was approved in 2017, for blood cancers. These treatments have produced long remissions in metastatic disease, but an overactive immune response can cause serious, even life-threatening, side effects.

links.note: Targeted drugs, the other route away from chemotherapy.

title: CRISPR gene editing

confidence.note: The 2012 paper, the 2020 Nobel Prize and the 2023 approvals are all on the record. Who deserves credit is genuinely contested: many laboratories contributed, and the patent fight between Berkeley and the Broad Institute ran for years.

place: Berkeley, USA; Vienna; Alicante; Vilnius; Cambridge, Massachusetts
people: Emmanuelle Charpentier, microbiologist, Nobel Prize 2020
Jennifer Doudna, biochemist, Nobel Prize 2020
Francisco Mojica, microbiologist at the University of Alicante
Virginijus Šikšnys, biochemist at Vilnius University
Feng Zhang, Broad Institute
He Jiankui, scientist jailed for editing embryos
summary: Two scientists turned a bacterial defense against viruses into scissors for DNA. Within a decade it had made a medicine, and a scandal.
body: In 2012 Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna showed how to turn part of a bacterial immune system into a programmable tool for cutting DNA. Studying *Streptococcus pyogenes*, Charpentier had found a previously unknown molecule, tracrRNA, that belongs to the bacterium's defense against viruses. Working with Doudna, she rebuilt the system in a test tube, simplified it, and proved that its enzyme, Cas9, could be steered to cut any DNA at a chosen site. Changing a gene, once a matter of months or years, could now take weeks.

The discovery stood on two decades of curiosity-driven microbiology. Researchers in Osaka noticed odd repeated sequences in *E. coli* DNA in 1987. Francisco Mojica in Alicante found similar ones in archaea in 1995 and was among the first to propose that they were part of a microbial immune system. Virginijus Šikšnys's group in Vilnius showed that a 20-letter stretch of guide RNA is enough to direct the cut. In January 2013 Feng Zhang at the Broad Institute and George Church at Harvard showed that the method worked in human cells, as did Doudna and others. Zhang's side won the first patent, in April 2014, beginning a long legal dispute.

The power of the tool was shown in the worst way in November 2018, when the Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced the birth of twin girls whose embryos he had edited to disable a gene called CCR5, hoping to make them resistant to HIV. In one twin the edit was incomplete. In December 2019 he was convicted of illegal medical practice and sentenced to three years in prison, and China later made illegal embryo editing a crime.

Charpentier and Doudna received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020. On 16 November 2023 Britain authorized Casgevy, the first licensed medicine made with CRISPR, for sickle-cell disease and β-thalassemia; the US followed on 8 December. In 2025 doctors in Philadelphia reported giving a baby with a rare, often fatal metabolic disease a base-editing therapy designed for his single mutation. It was a bespoke treatment for one child, and longer follow-up is still needed.

myth.tradition: CRISPR gene editing was invented by Charpentier and Doudna alone, in a single stroke in 2012.
myth.record: Their 2012 paper was the key step, but it built on work since 1987 by microbiologists such as Mojica and Šikšnys, and others, notably Zhang and Church, first showed editing in human cells. Priority was fought over for years in patent courts.

links.note: The first generation of tools for cutting and splicing DNA.

title: A cure for hepatitis C

confidence.note: The virus's identification, the drug approvals, the US launch price and Egypt's campaign figures are all documented; Egypt's numbers are official figures reported by WHO.

people: Michael Houghton, virologist, Nobel Prize 2020
Harvey J. Alter, Nobel Prize 2020
Charles M. Rice, Nobel Prize 2020
summary: A virus found in 1989 became curable with a short course of pills in 2013, at first for $84,000. Egypt showed what cheaper drugs could do.
body: For years most blood-borne hepatitis was caused by an unknown agent, called "non-A, non-B". In 1989 Michael Houghton's team isolated the genome of the hepatitis C virus, work honored with the 2020 Nobel Prize. Gilead's sofosbuvir, authorized in the United States in 2013, made cure possible with short courses of pills, but launched there at $84,000. Generics and price deals changed the picture. Egypt tested over 60 million people and treated more than 4.1 million, and in 2023 became the first country WHO rated "gold tier" on the path to elimination.

links.note: Another antiviral revolution, and another fight over drug prices.

title: Ebola in West Africa and a vaccine

confidence.note: WHO's case and death counts are the standard figures, though they include suspected cases and certainly miss some deaths. The vaccine trial results are published and widely accepted.

summary: An outbreak in a Guinean village killed over 11,000 people. A trial run in the middle of it proved a vaccine worked.
body: The epidemic was traced back to a two-year-old in Meliandou, Guinea, who died in December 2013. It spread to Liberia and Sierra Leone, and WHO declared an international emergency only on 8 August 2014. By the end WHO counted 28,616 confirmed, probable and suspected cases and 11,310 deaths. In 2015 a trial in coastal Guinea tested the rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine using ring vaccination, the strategy that eradicated smallpox: among 5,837 people vaccinated, no cases appeared ten days or more afterward, against 23 among the unvaccinated. The vaccine, Ervebo, was licensed in Europe in November 2019.

links.note: The virus's first recognized outbreaks, in Zaire and Sudan.
Ring vaccination was borrowed from the smallpox campaign.
